Household debt rose while the ratio fell: read the stock, income and payments separately

Explore twelve quarters of Canadian debt-to-income statistics, reconcile the debt components and build a separate household payment and cash-flow plan in six charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read the sector statistics, then test a separate household cash plan

Interactive planning lab

Entered debt / twelve months of net cash income437.50%
Scheduled payments / monthly net cash income35.00%
Monthly cash after the selected commitments$900

The first three figures are fixed public Statistics Canada observations from one reviewed vintage. The last three describe a separate hypothetical household with a different net-cash-income definition. Debt is a stock; income and payments are flows. The two personal ratios have different numerators and periods. Scheduled payments are entered independently; the model does not calculate a loan payment, interest rate, remaining term, underwriting limit or affordability verdict. It assumes constant monthly net cash income solely to show twelve months of receipts. No tax, new borrowing or investment return is modeled.

The central idea

A debt-to-income ratio compares an outstanding balance with an income flow. Required payments and the cash left for other commitments need their own calculations.

01

Start with the date and the two sides of the ratio

The reviewed Statistics Canada debt table reports a household credit-market debt-to-disposable-income ratio of 176.37% for 2026 Q2. The table was released on 11 September 2026 and retrieved for this article on 25 October 2026. This is a quarterly observation, rather than an October reading.

Its numerator is the seasonally adjusted stock of credit-market debt. Its denominator is household disposable income at a seasonally adjusted annual rate. For the latest quarter, those amounts are CAD 3,280,888 million and CAD 1,860,216 million. The calculation is 100 × 3,280,888 ÷ 1,860,216 = about 176.3713%, which rounds to the published 176.37%.

Equivalently, the sector owes about CAD 1.7637 for each dollar of that annualized income measure. This comparison does not say that households send 176.37% of their monthly receipts to lenders. The first figure follows this same defined ratio across twelve quarters, using a single reviewed vintage.

02

A falling ratio can coexist with a growing debt stock

The latest pair of observations makes the denominator visible. Between 2026 Q1 and Q2, the debt stock rises from CAD 3,252,456 million to CAD 3,280,888 million. Annualized disposable income rises from CAD 1,821,552 million to CAD 1,860,216 million.

Debt therefore increases by CAD 28,432 million, or about 0.87%, while the income measure increases by about 2.12%. Income grows faster proportionally, so the published ratio falls from 178.55% to 176.37%, a decrease of 2.18 percentage points. This arithmetic does not establish that any particular household reduced its borrowing.

The second chart rebases each underlying series to 100 in 2023 Q3. That common starting value lets you compare proportional changes across the displayed window. It does not equate the original dollar amounts. A debt stock remains a stock, and the income series remains an annualized flow.

03

Reconcile the balance before discussing borrowing or repayments

The third chart adds the latest debt-stock components in CAD billions: mortgage liabilities of 2,446.879, consumer credit of 678.683 and the separately classified non-mortgage loans of 155.326. Their sum is 3,280.888. The expandable data table retains three decimal places of billions to preserve the original million-dollar values.

The source’s credit-market-debt definition has a specific scope. Statistics Canada’s financial-accounts guide distinguishes it from broader household liabilities that also include trade payables. It also measures gross debt rather than subtracting a household’s assets to calculate net worth.

The same debt table separately records CAD 29.421 billion of net borrowing during Q2. That is a flow over the quarter. It is neither the CAD 3,280.888 billion stock still outstanding nor the gross contractual payments due. A change in stock can also include other changes in the accounts; do not force net borrowing to equal the difference between two balances.

04

Define a personal stock ratio and a payment ratio separately

The fourth chart starts again with a fictional household. It owes CAD 420,000 at a chosen date and receives CAD 8,000 a month of net cash income. Assuming that monthly amount continues for twelve months gives CAD 96,000 of receipts. Its explicitly defined debt-to-annual-net-cash-income ratio is 420,000 ÷ 96,000, or 437.5%.

The household separately enters CAD 2,800 of scheduled monthly debt payments, including principal and interest. That is 35% of its CAD 8,000 monthly net income. The outstanding balance does not uniquely determine that payment: rates, contract structure, remaining terms and any required lump sums also matter.

The 437.5% and 35% figures answer different questions. Neither reproduces the national statistic or a mortgage qualification calculation. The personal denominator is take-home cash; the national-accounts denominator has its own income and sector definitions. The model does not turn the stock ratio into a number of years until repayment, because it has not allocated all income to debt or calculated future interest.

05

Put the scheduled payment into the monthly cash plan once

The fifth chart uses the same CAD 8,000 of net income and CAD 2,800 of debt payments. It then subtracts CAD 4,000 of ordinary living costs and CAD 300 reserved monthly for CAD 3,600 of predictable annual bills. The result is CAD 900 of unallocated monthly cash.

Living costs exclude the debt payments and the listed annual bills. Entering the full loan payment in living costs and subtracting it again in the payment field would count the same commitment twice. The reserve also has a purpose: cash held for an upcoming bill cannot simultaneously fund another goal.

Keeping debt and income unchanged while increasing the entered scheduled payment to CAD 3,800 leaves a CAD 100 monthly shortfall. The stock-to-income ratio stays at 437.5%. This illustrates why the balance ratio alone cannot establish the cash available for food, housing, saving or an unexpected expense. Unlisted commitments still need their own review.

06

Read the stress grid as a cash sensitivity

The final chart changes receipts and scheduled payments independently. Its columns use 80%, 90%, 100% and 110% of entered monthly income. Rows use 80%, 100%, 120% and 140% of the entered payment. Living costs and the annual-bill reserve remain fixed.

With the starting assumptions, an income decline to CAD 6,400 and unchanged CAD 2,800 payments leaves a CAD 700 monthly funding gap. Combining that income with CAD 3,360 payments creates a CAD 1,260 gap. These cells are arithmetic scenarios; they are not estimated probabilities or an automatic translation from a change in market interest rates.

A lower payment also needs an actual contractual explanation before it becomes a workable plan. The grid does not grant a payment holiday, amend a loan, or show the later interest cost of extending repayment. It identifies which assumed cash combinations need additional funding or revised commitments.

07

Use the public indicator beside a dated household debt list

Record each personal balance as of a date, then separately record its required payment, timing and interest terms. The FCAC’s debt-assessment guidance recommends listing amounts owed, minimum monthly payments and interest rates, alongside a monthly budget.

Use the official charts to understand the sector measure and its revisions. Use the household charts to reconcile the selected cash commitments. Statistics Canada’s household sector includes unincorporated businesses, and its disposable-income definition goes beyond one employee’s pay deposit. An aggregate ratio of totals also cannot reveal the median household’s position or the distribution of burdens.

When updating the evidence, retain both table release dates and recheck their matching vintages. The documented methodology uses annual-rate income for this seasonally adjusted ratio. Multiplying debt by four or silently substituting an older moving-income denominator would produce a different measure. Keep the calculation defined before using its percentage to interpret a financial plan.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first three charts use public Statistics Canada observations for 2023 Q3–2026 Q2. The debt table was released 11 September 2026; the income table was released 28 August 2026. Both were retrieved 25 October 2026. The final three charts are hypothetical household calculations with a separate net-cash-income definition. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Household sector credit market summary, Table 38-10-0238-01 ↗

    Released 11 September 2026; retrieved 25 October 2026. Canada, seasonally adjusted, 2023 Q3–2026 Q2. Ratio vector v1038036698; credit-market debt-stock vector v1038036700. Six reviewed measures supply 72 original rows, including stock components and a separately defined financial flow. Historical observations may be revised.

  2. Statistics Canada · Current and capital accounts — Households, Table 36-10-0112-01 ↗

    Released 28 August 2026; retrieved 25 October 2026. Twelve matched household-disposable-income rows, Canada, seasonally adjusted at annual rates, vector v62305981. Both source CSV hashes are retained; all twelve rounded debt/income ratios and component sums were independently reconciled.

  3. Statistics Canada · National balance sheet and financial flow accounts, second quarter 2026 ↗

    11 September 2026 release. Confirms the latest debt/income observation, income growing faster than debt and the separate debt-service concept. Revised first-quarter values are used consistently from the retrieved vintage.

  4. Statistics Canada · Integrated seasonal adjustment of stocks and flows ↗

    2018 methodology, corrected in 2019. Documents seasonally adjusted debt divided by household disposable income at annual rates, replacing the earlier moving-income approach for this ratio. Used for definitions alongside the current tables, not for current numerical values.

  5. Statistics Canada · Financial and Wealth Accounts user guide, chapter 6 ↗

    Scope of credit-market debt and other liabilities. Stocks, flows and payment obligations retain separate definitions in this article.

  6. Statistics Canada · Canadian and U.S. household disposable-income reconciliation ↗

    Dated definition and institutional-scope explanation. The personal take-home-cash model is explicitly different from the official household-sector income concept.

  7. FCAC · Paying back your debt ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Supports listing each amount owed, minimum monthly payment and interest rate and reviewing income and spending. All individual-household amounts in this article are hypothetical assumptions.
